| Near full utilisation | Fails above freely available liquidity; withdrawal queue; per-interval cap | Fails above the shared, slowly expanding withdrawal limit | Fails on bank liquidity | Fails on liquidity; outflow rate limiter |
| Token-2022 lent mint | Yes, no hook, zero fee | Yes, no hook, zero fee | Yes (details unverified) | No |
| Devnet | Same program id, current, anyone can make a market | Stale programs; test on cloned mainnet | None at mainnet id | Separate old program |

## Prior art: Meteora's Dynamic Vault

- Meteora's Dynamic Vault is the closest prior art: a vault keeps liquidity in its token vault, an off-chain operator (Hermes) moves it in and out of lending strategies, and a user withdrawal can pull from a strategy first when the vault is short (`withdraw_directly_from_strategy`).
- In its current source the only external lending strategy with a working handler is Jupiter Lend; the Kamino, MarginFi and Solend variants remain in the enum but are unsupported (docs.meteora.ag Dynamic Vault pages, mirrored in the knowledge base at `raw/meteora-docs/pages/developer-guides__dynamic-vault__changelog.md` and `legacy-products__dynamic-vault__hermes__rebalance-crank.md`; the program source `mercurial-vault` is not public, so this rests on Meteora's docs).
- That choice fits a vault called at the top level, where Jupiter Lend's extra level costs nothing; our in-swap path is one level deeper, which is why it points the other way for us.
- Meteora's vault program is on klend's CPI whitelist (`utils/consts.rs` line 233), so Meteora could have used Kamino's obligations; we cannot.

## Corrections to earlier notes

- `research/estimates.md` says calling a lending market inside a swap of a hooked token exceeds the call-depth limit.
  It does not, for the lent side: the lending call and the hooked token's transfer are sibling calls under the strategy, and neither Kamino nor Jupiter Lend accepts a mint with a transfer hook, so the lent mint never carries one.
  The real limit is Jupiter Lend's withdraw at height 5 plus any extra outer level; Kamino's redeem stays at height 4.
- `research/estimates.md` says Kamino's devnet presence is unknown; klend is on devnet at its mainnet id, so a devnet demo is possible with our own lending market, and cloned mainnet state is needed only for tests against real reserves.

## Open questions for Lending pool design (#21)

1. Does a swap ever redeem from the lending market, or only spend the buffer while keeper jobs rebalance?
   If it redeems, the quote must read the reserve's freely available liquidity and withdrawal cap, and swaps above buffer plus that amount must fail cleanly.
2. Which mints are lent: only SOL (WSOL) and USDC, the side that has a Kamino main-market reserve?
3. Which reserve on mainnet (the main market's SOL reserve `d4A2prbA2whesmvHaL88BH6Ewn5N4bTSU2Ze8P6Bc4Q`?), and on devnet, our own lending market (what oracle config does its reserve need) or someone else's?
4. How does the market's price and each LP's share value the cTokens: at the reserve's exchange rate refreshed in the same call, or at the last keeper job's rate?
5. What does the lending pool do when the reserve is nearly fully borrowed (SOL was about 91% on 2026-11-09): raise the buffer, queue a withdrawal ticket, or stop lending?
6. What happens if Kamino sets `block_ctoken_usage` or emergency mode on our reserve: deposits stop in the first case, and in emergency mode redeems stop too, so swaps live on the buffer alone?
7. Do cToken holders miss Kamino's farm rewards, which attach to obligations (unverified)?
8. Should the strategy keep a lending-market adapter so Jupiter Lend can be added for keeper jobs later, or once SIMD-0268 raises the call-depth limit?
9. Test plan: a LiteSVM test of the in-swap redeem at one extra outer level (a smart-wallet trader), and a devnet demo against our own klend market.

## Sources

Code (read-only clones in a scratchpad):

- Pipeline `a2d5bfbe62ff61d3ca0ce7a976520da61a0f16c4`: `docs/ROUTER.md`, `docs/STRATEGY-GUIDE.md`, `docs/DEVNET.md`, `docs/INTEGRATOR-GUIDE.md` (https://github.com/MetalLegBob/pipeline).
- Kamino klend `686913ee421e0c5f3dc44c4c8344461ee0e4fb89` (release 1.28.0), files under `programs/klend/src/` as cited (https://github.com/Kamino-Finance/klend/tree/686913ee421e0c5f3dc44c4c8344461ee0e4fb89); handler history from `gh api repos/Kamino-Finance/klend/commits?path=programs/klend/src/handlers/handler_deposit_reserve_liquidity.rs`.
- Jupiter Lend integration guide `7960a14a5a760abc41db3ed1395dc5cb56a1f8db`: `docs/earn/cpi.md`, `README.md` (https://github.com/jup-ag/jupiter-lend).
- Fluid Solana programs `626b177f235224bc5d074d39439cd2558f542886`: `programs/lending`, `programs/liquidity`, `programs/flashloan`, `crates/library` as cited (https://github.com/Instadapp/fluid-solana-programs).
- MarginFi v2 `8665b8d1afc4d39bf7e575a85c663580e35c6314` (https://github.com/mrgnlabs/marginfi-v2).
- Save `d04ce00bbf4356c4fd32b3be38eb9760b696bb3e` (https://github.com/solendprotocol/solana-program-library).
- Surfpool (https://github.com/txtx/surfpool, README: a drop-in `solana-test-validator` replacement that mirrors mainnet state without a snapshot) and LiteSVM (https://github.com/LiteSVM/litesvm).

Knowledge base (`Research-Projects/jupiter-meteora`):

- `jupiter/03-lend-perps-predict-jupusd-dev.md` section 1 (Jupiter Lend programs, Earn CPI, devnet ids).
- `meteora/03-dev-dbc-vaults-launch.md` "Dynamic Vault" and the raw Meteora docs pages named above.

On chain and APIs (2026-11-09):

- Program existence and last-deploy slots: `getAccountInfo` on each program and its programdata, mainnet and `https://api.devnet.solana.com`.
- Kamino reserves: `getProgramAccounts` on klend filtered by size 8624 (and by lending market at offset 32), decoding the liquidity mint at offset 128, reserve status at 4856 and `block_ctoken_usage` at 4862, from the `Reserve` and `ReserveConfig` layouts in `state/reserve.rs`.
- Compute units: `getSignaturesForAddress` then `getTransaction` logs, for the USDC reserve `D6q6wuQSrifJKZYpR1M8R4YawnLDtDsMmWM1NbBmgJ59` (120 signatures) and the Jupiter Lend Lending program (120 signatures).
- `https://api.kamino.finance/kamino-market/7u3HeHxYDLhnCoErrtycNokbQYbWGzLs6JSDqGAv5PfF/reserves/metrics` and `https://api.jup.ag/lend/v1/earn/tokens` (both free and keyless).

documents.title: Pool4 on one Pipeline strategy, and what the `pool4.json` strategy is
documents.body:
Researched on 2026-11-09 for ticket #11; every fact below is as of that date.
Sources: IMD's docs at https://pool4.imd.fun/docs, the verified source of IMD's `CappedBurnHook` on Ethereum mainnet, Pipeline's source at commit `a2d5bfb` (read-only clone in a scratchpad, never copied here), and devnet accounts and transactions read through the free public RPC and Helius devnet.
Anything marked "inferred" was worked out from on-chain numbers, not read from source.

## Answer in brief

- Pool4 fits one Pipeline strategy whose quote and swap share one pricing function.
- The buy wall is a second liquidity segment on the SOL side only, so pricing is a two-segment curve with one boundary and no extra accounts.
- The trim and the cap ratchet can run inside `pipeline_swap` after the output is priced, as bookkeeping in the market state with no token movement, so they never change the quote and never touch the router's measurements.
- Burning, paying shares, placing the wall and sweeping fees become keeper jobs (custom actions).
- The `pool4.json` strategy (`4ajWF6Y3wsxXUbvvaEu7ZcA2RosB1YfaXcqot8kguwJD`) is not a four-mint pool.
  It is MetalLegBob's own Pool4 port for Solana: two mints (a Token-2022 token and wSOL), a trim to an inventory cap, a cap ratchet with a daily decay, a SOL buy wall that bought tokens on devnet, burns, keeper tips and a swept fee ledger (partly inferred from on-chain numbers, section 1).
  Its source is not public, its metadata URL is a placeholder, and it was registered on 2026-11-08.
- Measured compute in his port: 15.4k to 16.7k units for a buy, 12.9k to 14.2k for a sell that trims, 28.6k for a sell that fills the wall, against 8.8k to 12.0k for Pipeline's example constant-product strategy.

## 1. What the `pool4.json` strategy is

### Identity

- Program `4ajWF6Y3wsxXUbvvaEu7ZcA2RosB1YfaXcqot8kguwJD`: upgradeable loader, upgrade authority `2yJJsmhvs2SBsKVtiKCG4wBJNoTH67aRNMhSwkupvUHZ` (MetalLegBob's devnet authority, see `research/pipeline-router.md`), last deployed in slot 520151758 (2026-11-08 21:10 UTC), 450,216 bytes (`solana program show`, devnet).
- The router's `Strategy` record `DHrDdeG2MSFsWqqGJckiQ926AYguRHxVpBjgdaxgLBjn` (PDA `["strategy", program]` of the router) holds the metadata URI `https://example.com/pipeline/pool4.json`, a registration time of 1794134338 (2026-11-08 10:38:58 UTC) and a market count of 8 (raw account data, devnet).
- The registration transaction is `58MmzfapKPBenZ9v8Kwxt9CLsa9JrCeY4i9K3Fnw8EvJtbzHZ3zzmtgA7H3V6vJAamqsxzjo4ixJnRKgbsV49Xe5` (https://explorer.solana.com/tx/58MmzfapKPBenZ9v8Kwxt9CLsa9JrCeY4i9K3Fnw8EvJtbzHZ3zzmtgA7H3V6vJAamqsxzjo4ixJnRKgbsV49Xe5?cluster=devnet).
- Strings in the deployed binary (dumped with `solana program dump`) name it: the crate path `pool4/src/lib.rs`, the PDA seed `pool4-seeded`, the errors "Pool4 trades exact-in only", "The price is too far above the reference to rebalance", "The vaults no longer cover the pool's accounts" and "Caller is not this pool's Pipeline market", and the instructions `PipelineInitMarket`, `PipelineMarketInfo`, `PipelineResolveAccounts`, `PipelineQuote`, `PipelineSwap`, `PipelineSeedLiquidity`, `SeedPool`, `RebalanceWall`, `SettleRetired` and `SweepFees`.
- The census label "4-mint pool" in `research/pipeline-router.md` is wrong: `pipeline_market_info` returned two mints and `supports_exact_out: false` when market `F6f6xBPCT6ZxXPNuFwCrDwPH7pnNdZARFChuNUfVUeBF` was created (return data of transaction `3QxDnmP96s4diUdqyKjLGXpD65fd79bkakce1JqdkMVcG3q6B1YX4WPTUkyErhpBdKJsmSYKV2n4dS7AyreRZPA9`).
  "pool4" is the design's name, not a mint count.

### How its markets are made

- All 8 markets were created by MetalLegBob's bonding-curve strategy (`ETrmUegraeyB7B6fXBfANmV7w9aEwM3wUEUzFHqo5zAb`, crate `bonding-curve`) in its `Graduate` instruction, which calls the Pool4 strategy's `pipeline_seed_liquidity` and then the router's `register_existing_market` (logs of the 8 seeding transactions, devnet).
- So the path is a bonding-curve launch that graduates straight into a Pool4 market (Seeding in our glossary); the seed returned `SeedResult { taken: [211111111111112, 5045600000], lp_amount: 0 }` for market `F6f6x...`, so there are no LP shares and the liquidity is owned by the market.
- The token mints are Token-2022 (`TokenzQdBNbLqP5VEhdkAS6EPFLC1PHnBqCXEpPxuEb`), the other side is wSOL.
- 23 of the strategy's 31 transactions were paid by `2yJJsmhv...`, 5 by `39zx59wehvSfocr5VY6KfesDJD2Bpto5BQ5mH4L6218o` (which also received the keeper tips and a 0.01 SOL payment in a seeding transaction), 2 by `vbKLAhRD...` and 1 by `BJZJJkqJ...`; the trades look like scripted tests in four sessions on 2026-11-08 (10:38, 11:31, 13:20 and 21:10 UTC).
- The market state grew from 567 to 591 to 623 bytes across those sessions, so the layout was still changing (`getProgramAccounts` on the program, devnet).

### What it does, replayed from one market

Market `F6f6xBPCT6ZxXPNuFwCrDwPH7pnNdZARFChuNUfVUeBF` ran a full lifecycle on 2026-11-08 between 11:31:10 and 11:32:36 UTC; the numbers below are token balance changes from its transactions, replayed against a model in a scratchpad script.

| Step | Transaction | What moved |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Seed | `3QxDnmP96s...` | 211,111,111,111,112 token units and 5,045,600,000 lamports into the vaults |
| Sell | `34rPsixBFz...` | 6,217,190,650,882 tokens in (after the Pipeline fee), 143,424,712 lamports out |
| Buy | `4hJuwN81aB...` | 50,000,000 lamports in, 2,179,198,988,285 tokens out |
| RebalanceWall | `5NDTC4ijPb...` | no vault change except a 307,025-lamport tip to the caller |
| Sell into the wall | `4mL2xTo17E...` | 2,751,850,564,892 tokens in, 62,198,306 lamports out |
| RebalanceWall | `5PhVCpuRqa...` | a 30,635-lamport tip to the caller |
| SettleRetired | `cVEHucgUyg...` | 6,803,005,463,489 tokens left the token vault: 14,966,612,019 to the caller, the rest burned |
| SweepFees | `2JLPsh1v49...` | 44,845,206,080 tokens and 250,000 lamports to the fee recipient stored in the market state |

Full signatures: `3QxDnmP96s4diUdqyKjLGXpD65fd79bkakce1JqdkMVcG3q6B1YX4WPTUkyErhpBdKJsmSYKV2n4dS7AyreRZPA9`, `34rPsixBFznxvqbsSVuWVFXksSfGsoJNUEGhUFdkYybDyUaVtCd9eXR6ekHzAFR3wYea8FbRZNfYYdFR3UDj7MLU`, `4hJuwN81aBX5iM5hhxmvCpj69kG9HBPkD4jrZPJRTZ8kTDkru57N6c4bhHYMPze2i1iU7mr8Az4uzzd6rNiWXQ9Q`, `5NDTC4ijPb1aFo5MwoMJvQbG8bvFj53uNRKghdvR6L26XP7f8AmDqUs4DL6Q6eT5fFwPqMvmvKFLJZUQ4Jwogs7f`, `4mL2xTo17EU7E1m5KnH6XWv9sAmwLW4Z9fhDWoP2dYH4Dpe6Gv2NiKbpS7GbB2PNnfdxSpq8KCy3o5F4JBK4mHGL`, `5PhVCpuRqaTKbp7xzzgt6rucnityYzRE91K2fDHMDX7bTWtE6FjcndS3hFKftuanCcRR7Xtm5yArvxCfhM9XigQH`, `cVEHucgUygEb5dDvdcXmnCAJLzjgi7vEiTxMCJydVTvHuRqBLjUxDz77VAJzde62qbh74mpFBLiTkg4BiDeodWf`, `2JLPsh1v49BX3bKyfnC48ptGHba3yujdDsdqPpBNhHTGmjf2CGCCxYToE4gtAKWCMaQ6wRVdVeTD12QUGUS2MRjU` (devnet).

What the replay shows:

- Pricing is constant product, exact-in only, with two fees.
  A fee of 50 basis points of the input, rounded up, goes to a fee ledger that `SweepFees` pays out (the swept 44,845,206,080 tokens equal the two sells' rounded-up 50 basis points exactly, and the swept 250,000 lamports equal 50 basis points of the buy).
  A second fee of 15 basis points is always taken in SOL and stays in the pool: from the SOL output on a sell and from the SOL input on a buy.
  With these rules the model reproduces the sell's 143,424,712 lamports and the buy's 2,179,198,988,285 tokens to the unit (inferred from the replay; the rule is not in any published source).
- The trim is real and does not move the price.
  The buy only reproduces exactly if, after the first sell, token inventory was cut back to the inventory cap (the seeded 211,111,111,111,112) together with the proportional SOL (139,557,101 lamports) at an unchanged price (inferred).
- The trim moves no tokens inside the swap.
  `PipelineSwap` makes only the output transfer; the trimmed SOL stays in the wSOL vault as buy-wall SOL and the trimmed tokens stay in the token vault until `SettleRetired` burns them (logs of the swap and settle transactions).
  At the end the wSOL vault held exactly the curve's SOL plus the wall's SOL (4,764,094,889 + 125,294,433 = 4,889,389,322 lamports, from the market state and the vault balance).
- The cap ratchet with a daily decay is implemented.
  After the buy the stored cap is 211,110,908,307,615, which is the seeded cap minus `floor(211,111,111,111 x 83 / 86,400)` = 202,803,497, so the cap fell by a decay of 211,111,111,111 tokens a day (0.1% of the seeded inventory) over the 83 seconds from seeding to the next sell; 211,111,111,111 appears twice in the state, consistent with a cap floor equal to one day's decay, as in IMD's launch values (cap floor 1,000 IMD, cap decay 1,000 IMD a day) (inferred from the market state).
  The decay ran to the second sell's time, not the buy's, so the port applies the ratchet at a different point than IMD's hook, which ratchets only right after a swap that left inventory below the cap (inferred).
- The buy wall filled.
  The first `RebalanceWall` placed 139,250,076 lamports (the trim's SOL less the tip); the second sell paid out about 13,925,008 lamports of it as the price fell into the wall; the second `RebalanceWall` retired what the wall bought; 125,294,433 lamports remained (inferred from the tips and the final state).
  The sell that filled the wall cost 28,562 compute units against 12,890 to 14,188 for other sells.
- Keeper tips: both `RebalanceWall` tips and the `SettleRetired` tip are 0.22% of the work done (307,025 of 139,557,101 lamports; 30,635 of 13,925,008 lamports; 14,966,612,019 of 6,803,005,463,489 tokens), paid to the caller; two stored parameters equal 10,000,000 and 2,000,000 lamports, consistent with a rebalance threshold of 0.01 SOL and a tip ceiling of 0.002 SOL (inferred; IMD's are 0.1 ETH and 0.002 ETH).
- `RebalanceWall` refuses when the price is too far above a reference ("The price is too far above the reference to rebalance"), a guard against pumping the price before placing the wall; IMD's hook uses a placement floor instead (section 2).

## 2. IMD's Pool4 mechanics, from the verified hook

Read from the verified source of `CappedBurnHook` at `0xc6c965bd164c483e87d0b550671798e9a3602840` on Ethereum mainnet (Solidity 0.8.30, verified 2026-09-19; https://sourcify.dev/server/v2/contract/1/0xc6c965bd164c483e87d0b550671798e9a3602840?fields=sources, also https://etherscan.io/address/0xc6c965bd164c483e87d0b550671798e9a3602840#code).
Constructor arguments: `rewardShareBps` 1500, `minTrimTokens` 0, `lpFee` 10000 (1% in v4's millionths), `tickSpacing` 60.

- Every swap runs `afterSwap`, which collects this swap's LP fee into a separate fee ledger, then `_applyCap`, then `_updateDeploymentFloor`, then `_observeTick`; it declares no deltas, so the quote is plain Uniswap v4 maths.
- `_applyCap` reads the tokens held by the full-range position.
  If they are below the cap, the cap ratchets: `next = cap - (cap - held) x ratchetBps / 10,000`, no lower than `cap - capDecayTokensPerDay x elapsed / 1 day` and no lower than `capFloor`; the decay clock then advances by the time-equivalent of what was used, with a carried remainder so many tiny ratchets cannot beat the rate.
  If they are above the cap by at least `minTrimTokens`, it removes `liquidity x excess / held` from the position, which is price-neutral, and reverts if the price moved (`_requirePriceUnchanged`).
- Trimmed tokens are split `rewardShareBps` (at most 30%) to the rewards recipient and the rest to the burn sink; trimmed ETH goes to `retainedEth`, the buy wall's budget.
  Because v4 settles only at the end of the unlock, all of these are first held as ERC-6909 claims and turned into transfers later by `settleClaims` (a keeper job, or automatically in a later block).
- The buy wall (the hook calls it the backstop) is one single-sided ETH position from just past the price to the end of the price range, so it bids at every price from its top down to almost zero; while the price is inside it, the pool's liquidity is the full-range position plus the wall's.
- Only the permissionless `rebalance()` moves the wall: it closes the old wall, retires the tokens it bought through the same split, and places all retained ETH again, when idle ETH reaches `rebalanceEthThreshold` or the wall has converted that much.
  The keeper's tip is at most `keeperReward` and at most the pool fee on the work, so faking work never pays.
- The wall's top can be no higher in token price than `deploymentFloorTick`, which moves at once to any price the pool trades at and recovers only `floorDecayTicksPerDay` (400 ticks, about 4% a day, with elapsed time clipped to one day) toward `refTick`.
  `refTick` follows the previous block's closing tick by at most `maxRefStep` (200 ticks) per block, so one transaction cannot move it.
- The cap decay's elapsed time is not clipped, so idle days are banked for the next buy; the floor decay's is clipped to one day (both from the source).
- IMD's docs contradict themselves on launches: section 09 says a permissionless launch factory "is the plan, not a product yet", while section 13 says one transaction deploys a `CappedBurnHook` for any token at `/launch` (https://pool4.imd.fun/docs, read 2026-11-09); `research/pool4.md` repeats only the first.

## 3. Fitting Pool4 into one Pipeline strategy

### One pure function for quote and swap

Pipeline requires quote and swap to agree and suggests computing both from one function (`docs/STRATEGY-GUIDE.md`, rule 1, commit `a2d5bfb`, https://github.com/MetalLegBob/pipeline/blob/a2d5bfb/docs/STRATEGY-GUIDE.md).
The clean shape is `step(state, trade, clock) -> (QuoteResult, next_state)`: `pipeline_quote` returns the `QuoteResult`, and `pipeline_swap` checks the market signer, credits the input, calls the same `step`, pays out and writes `next_state`.
The trader's output is decided before the trim and the ratchet run, as in IMD's `afterSwap`, so they change the next trade's depth but never this trade's quote.
If any time-based change ran before pricing (a lazy decay that trims first, for example), the quote would depend on the clock, and the quoter would have to be given the expected time (`Quoter::set_clock`, `crates/pipeline-quoter/src/lib.rs`, commit `a2d5bfb`); keeping every time-based change after pricing avoids that.

### Constant product plus the buy wall

- Store the full-range position as liquidity `L` and the square-root price, as Uniswap does; the wall is a second liquidity `L_w` that is active below its top price.
- A sell moves the price down with `1/sqrtP' = 1/sqrtP + dx / L`, a buy moves it up with `sqrtP' = sqrtP + dy / L`; if a sell crosses the wall's top, the rest uses `L + L_w`.
  Because the wall reaches down to almost zero, there are at most two segments and one boundary, so the loop is bounded at two steps.
- Swaps need no square root and no tick arrays: only multiply-divides on 128 or 256 bits, as in the reference strategy's `mul_div` (`programs/test-strategy-cp/src/lib.rs`, commit `a2d5bfb`).
- Placing the wall needs `L_w = wall SOL / sqrtP_top` when its bottom is zero; that runs in the keeper job, not in the swap.
- The wall's SOL can sit in the same wSOL vault as the curve's, so the swap needs no account beyond the output vault; MetalLegBob's port does this (its swaps resolve exactly one strategy account, the output vault).
- Exact-out across the boundary is possible but adds an inverse for each segment; MetalLegBob's port is exact-in only, and integrators must honour `supports_exact_out: false`.

### The trim, without moving the price

- After pricing a sell, if the curve's tokens exceed the inventory cap, scale the full-range position by `cap / held` (both reserves, or `L`, by the same ratio); the price is unchanged.
- Book the removed tokens to a ledger of tokens awaiting burn and split (MetalLegBob's "retired") and the removed SOL to the wall's idle SOL; nothing moves in the swap.
- This keeps the input in the input vault, which the router asks of strategies (`docs/STRATEGY-GUIDE.md`, rule 10).
  Burning inside the swap would not cut the Pipeline fee, because the router charges on the larger of what the trader spent and what the vault kept (`settlement::settle` in `crates/pipeline-strategy-interface/src/lib.rs`, commit `a2d5bfb`), but it would add a burn and transfers to every sell and run any transfer hook at the deepest call level.
- Because the vaults then hold more than the curve's reserves, pass the sum of everything booked against a vault (reserves, fee ledger, retired tokens, wall SOL) as the "recorded reserve" to `credited_input`; passing only the curve's reserve makes `credited_input` return `amount_sent` even when a Token-2022 transfer fee took part of it, and the books drift above the vault (`credited_input` in `crates/pipeline-strategy-interface/src/lib.rs`).
  MetalLegBob's port checks the same invariant ("The vaults no longer cover the pool's accounts").

### The cap ratchet, floor and decay

- After pricing a buy, if the curve's tokens are below the cap, lower the cap by IMD's rule: the room the buy opened, times the ratchet share, limited by the decay allowance since the last ratchet and by the cap floor, with the decay clock and remainder carried as in the hook.
- It needs only the market state and the Clock sysvar, which Pipeline allows (`docs/STRATEGY-GUIDE.md`, rule 3).
- Run it in every swap, as IMD does in every `afterSwap`; leaving it to a keeper would let a sell and a buy in one transaction round-trip without ratcheting or trimming.

### The wall's guards

- IMD's guard needs a per-swap observation: the previous block's closing price, followed at a capped step, and a placement floor that drops at once and recovers about 4% a day.
- On Solana use the slot for the block, and keep these values as square-root prices with a fixed per-day ratio rather than ticks, so no logarithm is needed in the swap; 400 ticks a day is a ratio of `1.0001^200` a day on the square-root price.
- MetalLegBob's port instead refuses `RebalanceWall` when the price is too far above a reference; which guard we use is a design choice.

### Keeper jobs (custom actions)

| Job | Does | Called by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Place the wall | Retires what the wall bought, places idle SOL under the price, pays a tip | Anyone, when idle SOL or the wall's fill passes a threshold |
| Settle | Burns the retired tokens and pays the shares | Anyone |
| Sweep fees | Pays the fee ledger to its recipients | Anyone |

They are ordinary instructions on the strategy, called directly, with no Pipeline fee (`docs/STRATEGY-GUIDE.md`, section 5); each should be described in the strategy metadata's `actions` so Pipescope can render a form.

## 4. Compute

Measured on devnet on 2026-11-08 and 2026-11-09 from the transactions' logs; "strategy" is the units the strategy itself consumed inside the router's call.

| Instruction | Strategy | Units | Count |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `pipeline_swap`, buy (with the ratchet) | Pool4 port | 15,374 to 16,682 | 7 |
| `pipeline_swap`, sell (with a trim) | Pool4 port | 12,890 to 14,188 | 4 |
| `pipeline_swap`, sell that filled the wall | Pool4 port | 28,562 | 1 |
| `pipeline_swap` | example constant product `yRptCdde...` | 8,799 to 12,024 | 12 |
| Router `swap`, whole instruction | Pool4 port | 40,710 to 47,077 (62,629 with the wall) | 12 |
| `RebalanceWall` | Pool4 port | 10,805 to 10,820 | 2 |
| `SettleRetired` (includes a Token-2022 `TransferChecked` of 2,977 and a `Burn` of 2,397) | Pool4 port | 15,625 to 15,809 | 4 |
| `SweepFees` | Pool4 port | 20,307 | 1 |
| `pipeline_seed_liquidity` (creates the vaults) | Pool4 port | 71,047 to 86,047 | 8 |

What this means for each mechanism (inferred from the comparison, not measured separately):

- The trim and the ratchet as bookkeeping cost a few thousand units at most: a Pool4 sell with a trim costs about the same as an example-strategy swap plus the larger state.
- Filling the wall roughly doubles the strategy's cost (about 14k to 16k more in his port), still far under the quoter's default cap of 200,000 units (`docs/STRATEGY-GUIDE.md`, rule 7) and the about 1.3M units left for strategies per transaction.
- A quote should cost about the swap minus its token transfer; no quote is recorded on chain, so this is unverified.
- Doing the burn and two share transfers inside every trimming sell would add about 8k to 11k units (one `Burn` plus two `TransferChecked` at the measured costs) and a transfer-hook call for each transfer.

## 5. Recommendation

- Pool4 for Solana is feasible as one strategy, with the design in section 3: one pure `step` function, a two-segment square-root-price curve, the trim and ratchet as in-swap bookkeeping after pricing, the wall's SOL in the quote vault, and placement, settlement and fee sweeps as keeper jobs; start exact-in only.

## Sources

- IMD's docs: https://pool4.imd.fun/docs (read 2026-11-09).
- `CappedBurnHook` verified source: https://sourcify.dev/server/v2/contract/1/0xc6c965bd164c483e87d0b550671798e9a3602840?fields=sources and https://etherscan.io/address/0xc6c965bd164c483e87d0b550671798e9a3602840#code.
- Pipeline at commit `a2d5bfb` (2026-11-09 07:14 UTC): `docs/STRATEGY-GUIDE.md`, `crates/pipeline-strategy-interface/src/lib.rs` (`credited_input`, `settlement::settle`, `MAX_MARKET_MINTS`), `programs/test-strategy-cp/src/lib.rs`, `crates/pipeline-quoter/src/lib.rs` (`set_clock`); https://github.com/MetalLegBob/pipeline/tree/a2d5bfb.
- Devnet: program `4ajWF6Y3wsxXUbvvaEu7ZcA2RosB1YfaXcqot8kguwJD` (account, binary, 8 market states, all 31 transactions), program `ETrmUegraeyB7B6fXBfANmV7w9aEwM3wUEUzFHqo5zAb` (binary strings), router `Strategy` record `DHrDdeG2MSFsWqqGJckiQ926AYguRHxVpBjgdaxgLBjn`, and 25 recent transactions of `yRptCdde1du1JYR2DcNFtLC1fkp5Asd6rE3XSvZoUFx`; through `https://api.devnet.solana.com` and Helius devnet.

documents.title: Where the quoter runs for Canary checks
documents.body:
Researched 2026-11-09 for [#7](/7/), which feeds [Pipescope architecture](/13/).
Pipeline's source was read from a scratchpad clone of https://github.com/MetalLegBob/pipeline at commit `a2d5bfb` (2026-11-09 07:14 UTC); file paths below are inside that clone unless they start with `/`.
Cloudflare facts come from the owner's knowledge base at `Research-Projects/cloudflare`, a snapshot dated 2026-10-05, with the official page each fact came from.
Every measurement below was made on 2026-11-09 on the owner's Mac (x86_64, 20 cores, macOS 15) with Pipeline's pinned toolchain, Rust 1.97.1.

## Answer

- Run Canary checks as native Rust in a Cloudflare Container: it builds, it runs the router and a real devnet strategy correctly, it needs about 35 MB of memory, and at our volume it costs nothing beyond the $5 a month Workers Paid plan.
- A WASM build inside a Worker is ruled out: it does not build without a wasm C compiler, it does not run without patching an Agave crate, and once both are worked around the full router swap still fails inside the 32-bit wasm VM, so the exit test cannot run there.
- A small server elsewhere works as well as a Container (native, with the JIT) and costs about the same, but it adds a second platform, a second home for the RPC key and a public endpoint to guard.
- The quoter never fetches data itself; each Canary run takes a snapshot from devnet RPC (about ten calls, about 0.9 MB, mostly program bytes) and a new strategy version is detected by the `slot` in the strategy's ProgramData header.

## What the quoter is and needs

- `pipeline-quoter` wraps one `LiteSVM` (`litesvm = "=0.18.2"`) with signature and blockhash checks off and a funded payer (`crates/pipeline-quoter/Cargo.toml`; `crates/pipeline-quoter/src/lib.rs` lines 137 and 150).
- "The quoter never talks to the network": callers load programs with `load_program_from_program_data`, accounts with `set_account` and time with `set_clock` (`src/lib.rs` lines 4 to 6, 184, 198, 225).
- `quote` runs only the strategy's `pipeline_quote`; `simulate_swap` runs the whole router `swap` for a synthetic trader and reads the router's own result, so it needs the router program, its config, the market, the market's fee account and every account the swap touches (`src/lib.rs` lines 422 and 483).
- Strategy code runs under a compute cap, 200,000 units by default (`src/lib.rs` line 34).
- `simulate_swap` only simulates; the quoter keeps its `LiteSVM` private and has no way to commit a swap (`src/lib.rs` lines 137 and 483 to 544).
  The exit test buys and then sells back with the clock moved forward, so the Canary harness has to drive `litesvm` directly with `send_transaction` (reusing `pipeline-client`'s builders), not only the `Quoter` API; that harness has the same dependencies and so the same hosting answer.
- The integrator guide says to reload a program when its ProgramData changes, since strategies can be upgraded (`docs/INTEGRATOR-GUIDE.md` line 34).
- `pipeline-quoter` depends on 330 crates (`cargo tree -p pipeline-quoter -e normal`, unique name and version), including Agave's program runtime, the sBPF VM (`solana-sbpf 0.23.0`) and C code: `blst` (BLS12-381) through `solana-bls12-381-syscall` and `solana-bls-signatures`, which `litesvm` always pulls in (`cargo tree -i blst`).
- The sBPF VM uses its JIT only on x86_64 outside Windows (`solana-sbpf-0.23.0/src/lib.rs` line 38; `solana-program-runtime 4.3.2` enables the `jit` feature); wasm32 and arm64 hosts fall back to the interpreter.
- LiteSVM's own Node package (`litesvm` 1.6.2 on npm) is a napi native addon, not wasm, so it cannot run in a Worker either (https://github.com/LiteSVM/litesvm/blob/master/crates/node-litesvm/package.json).

## What we measured

A throwaway probe crate (kept in the session scratchpad, not in this repo) recorded one live devnet market of MetalLegBob's example constant-product strategy and ran it through the quoter, natively and as wasm.
All RPC was read-only on the public devnet endpoint; no transaction was sent.

### Devnet data for one market

- `getProgramAccounts` on the router filtered by the `Market` discriminator returned 43 markets on 2026-11-09 about 08:00 UTC: 19 on `yRptCdde...` (constant product), 12 on `ETrmUegr...` (bonding curve), 8 on `4ajWF6Y3...` (4-mint pool), 4 on `9mAV3pMK...` (outside builder); `research/pipeline-router.md` counted 38 earlier the same day.
- That call failed three times with HTTP 429 "Connection rate limits exceeded" on `https://api.devnet.solana.com` and took 108 s to succeed.
- Market `LCHsnkMfToU5C9G28JikT3eP3AvnCZSsPUeYvVLBS52` needed 9 accounts (market, market state, 2 mints, 2 vaults, router config, 2 fee accounts) plus the router's and the strategy's ProgramData; `pipeline_resolve_accounts` asked for one strategy account, already among them.
- Program bytes dominate: the router's ELF is 587,412 bytes and the strategy's 329,160 bytes; the whole snapshot serialised to 919,339 bytes.
- Fetching both ProgramData accounts took 1.1 s and the market's accounts 0.25 s.

### Native build (x86_64, JIT)

- `cargo build --release -p pipeline-quoter` succeeded in 4 min 16 s from cold.
- `Quoter::new` took 15 to 18 ms; a process holding only a new quoter peaked at 13.5 MB resident (`/usr/bin/time -l`).
- Loading the router, the strategy and 9 accounts took 7.6 ms; `resolve_accounts` 0.4 to 3 ms.
- `quote` took 160 µs each over 2,000 quotes in both directions.
  The integrator guide says 10 to 20 µs for simple strategies (`docs/INTEGRATOR-GUIDE.md` line 32); why ours is slower is not verified (each quote is a full simulated transaction, which may be the cost).
- `simulate_swap` of a buy succeeded and matched the quote exactly (`received` 208,888 for 763,013,620,993 in); 500 simulations averaged 0.68 ms each.
- `simulate_swap` of the sell direction failed with router error 6002 (`0x1772`), while its quote succeeded.
  In the `a2d5bfb` source error 6002 is `ListingFeeTooHigh` (`programs/pipeline/src/lib.rs` line 1287), which a swap cannot raise, so the router deployed on devnet probably differs from that source (unverified).
- The process peaked at 33.6 MB resident after all of it.

### wasm32-unknown-unknown (what a Worker runs)

- `cargo check --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` fails first in `getrandom 0.3.4`, which needs `--cfg getrandom_backend="wasm_js"` on that target.
- With that set it fails in `blst 0.3.17`'s build script: `clang` reports "No available targets are compatible with triple wasm32-unknown-unknown"; Apple's clang and the Solana platform-tools clang (v1.57) both lack the wasm backend, and none other is installed here.
- With the C step stubbed out (a no-op compiler, for checking only), the whole quoter type-checks for wasm32, so the Rust code itself compiles.
- `spl-token-2022-interface` turns on `getrandom 0.2`'s `js` feature for wasm32, so a real build also needs `wasm-bindgen` glue, as `workers-rs` uses anyway.
- Linked with `blst`'s symbols left as imports (38 of them), the module is 7.5 MB uncompressed including the 0.9 MB snapshot; the Worker size limit is 64 MiB uncompressed (https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/limits/).
- It traps in `Quoter::new`: `std::time::Instant::now` panics on this target, called from `solana_program_runtime::invoke_context::InvokeContext::process_message` through `solana-svm-measure 4.3.2` (`src/measure.rs` line 17) during `LiteSVM::airdrop`.
  Every transaction LiteSVM runs goes through that path; fixing it means patching `solana-svm-measure` (the only crate on the runtime path that reads the clock) and carrying that patch through every Agave upgrade.

### wasm32-wasip1 (wasm with a clock)

- To see how the quoter behaves as wasm once the clock works, the same probe was built for `wasm32-wasip1` and run in Node 26.9 with a six-call WASI shim.
- `Quoter::new` took 29 ms, loading 5.5 ms, `resolve_accounts` 8.7 ms, and `quote` 217 µs each, with 15.6 MB of linear memory.
- `simulate_swap` of the same buy that succeeds natively failed inside the router: "Access violation reading 32 bytes at address 0xcce8 (in unallocated region)".
  Quotes make no cross-program calls and work; the router swap makes several (the strategy, token programs, its event self-call), and fails on the 32-bit host; the root cause was not investigated.
- Workers' WASI support is "experimental ... with only some syscalls implemented" (https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/webassembly/), so this build would not be the way into a Worker anyway.

## The three options

| | Cloudflare Container | WASM in a Worker | Small server elsewhere |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Builds | Yes, native linux/amd64 image | No: needs a wasm C compiler for `blst`, `wasm-bindgen` glue and a getrandom flag | Yes, native |
| Runs Canary checks | Yes, with the JIT (x86_64) | No: clock panic without an Agave patch; router swaps fail in 32-bit wasm even with a clock | Yes, with the JIT on x86_64, interpreter on arm64 |
| Memory | About 35 MB measured; `basic` gives 1 GiB | 128 MB per isolate including the JS heap | About 35 MB; 256 MB machines are enough |
| CPU | `basic` is 1/4 vCPU; a run of a few hundred simulated swaps is well under a second of CPU at 0.7 ms each | 30 s default, 5 min max per request | Shared vCPU |
| Cold start | "often in the 1-3 second range" | Under 1 s startup limit; compile of a 7.5 MB module took 13 to 34 ms in Node | None if always on; about a minute on Render's free tier |
| Data from devnet | Fetches by RPC itself, or receives a snapshot from the Worker | Would get bytes from the Worker's `fetch` | Fetches by RPC itself |
| Monthly cost at our volume | $0 beyond Workers Paid ($5) | Would be $0 beyond Workers Paid, if it worked | From $2.19 (Fly.io) |

Sources for the table: Containers limits and instance types (https://developers.cloudflare.com/containers/platform/limits/), cold starts and linux/amd64 (https://developers.cloudflare.com/containers/concepts/architecture/), Workers memory, CPU and startup limits (https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/limits/), Fly.io and Render prices (`Research-Projects/cloudflare/alternatives.md` sections 3.6 and 3.8, from https://docs.fly.io/about/pricing and https://render.com/docs/free).

### Cloudflare Container

- Containers run any linux/amd64 image as part of a Workers app; each instance is a Firecracker microVM reached through its own Durable Object (https://developers.cloudflare.com/containers/, https://developers.cloudflare.com/containers/concepts/architecture/).
- They need the Workers Paid plan; there is no free allowance (KB `build/01-compute.md` section 3, Status).
- Instance types range from `lite` (1/16 vCPU, 256 MiB) to `standard-4` (4 vCPU, 12 GiB); `basic` is 1/4 vCPU, 1 GiB and 4 GB of disk (https://developers.cloudflare.com/containers/platform/limits/).
- There is no fixed maximum runtime, but hosts can restart instances at any time, and an instance that runs out of memory restarts; there is no swap (https://developers.cloudflare.com/containers/faq/).
- Containers can reach the internet by default; `enableInternet = false` with `allowedHosts` or an outbound handler limits it, and outbound handlers can inject auth headers, so the Helius key can stay in the Worker (https://developers.cloudflare.com/containers/configuration/outbound-traffic/).
- Scaling is manual today: address instances by id, or spread work over N instances with `getRandom` (https://developers.cloudflare.com/containers/configuration/scaling-and-routing/).

### WASM in a Worker

- Rust Workers compile to `wasm32-unknown-unknown` with `workers-rs` (https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/languages/rust/).
- Each isolate gets 128 MB including the JavaScript heap and WebAssembly allocations, shared by concurrent requests (https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/limits/).
- Workers disallow timers for security, so even a patched clock would read the same time throughout a request unless I/O happens (https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/languages/rust/crates/, citing https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/reference/security-model/).
- Making it work would mean a wasm C toolchain for `blst`, a fork of `solana-svm-measure`, and debugging Agave's VM on a 32-bit host, then repeating all three at each LiteSVM or Agave upgrade; it would also lose the JIT.

### Small server elsewhere

- Fly.io's cheapest always-on machine, `shared-cpu-1x` with 256 MB, is $2.19 per 30 days plus $0.02/GB egress; Fly.io has no free tier (`alternatives.md` section 3.6, from https://docs.fly.io/about/pricing).
- Railway's Hobby plan has a $5 monthly minimum; Render's free web services spin down after 15 minutes idle and take about a minute to wake (`alternatives.md` sections 3.7 and 3.8).
- Any of these runs the same native binary as the Container; the difference is operational, not technical.

## Cost at our volume

Assumptions: 50 strategy versions and a few hundred re-runs a month, rounded up to 500 Canary runs; each run is a cold start (worst case), about 10 s of work and 2 minutes of idle before the instance sleeps, on a `basic` instance.
That is about 133 s of billed running time per run, 18.5 hours a month.

| Dimension | Used | Included with Workers Paid | Overage cost |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Memory (1 GiB provisioned) | 18.5 GiB-hours | 25 GiB-hours | $0 |
| CPU (active only) | under 45 vCPU-minutes | 375 vCPU-minutes | $0 |
| Disk (4 GB provisioned) | 74 GB-hours | 200 GB-hours | $0 |
| Egress | well under 1 GB | 1 TB (North America and Europe) | $0 |

- Rates and allowances: https://developers.cloudflare.com/containers/platform/pricing/ (memory $0.0000025 per GiB-second, CPU $0.000020 per vCPU-second, disk $0.00000007 per GB-second beyond the allowance).
- Even a `standard-1` instance (4 GiB) would go 49 GiB-hours over, about $0.44 a month.
- The fronting Worker and the container's Durable Object are billed separately at their own rates (https://developers.cloudflare.com/containers/platform/pricing/).
  The Worker's few thousand requests a month sit inside Workers Paid's 10 million requests and 30 million CPU-ms (https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/pricing/).
  The Durable Objects' 500 runs of about 133 s, billed at 128 MB, come to about 8,300 GB-s against 400,000 GB-s and 1 million requests included a month (https://developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/platform/pricing/).
- So the cost of Canary checks is the $5 Workers Paid subscription, which Containers require and which the owner must approve before it is bought.

## Getting fresh account data from devnet

- Per Canary run, take a snapshot: the strategy's and the router's ProgramData, the market account, its market state, mints, vaults, the router config and fee accounts, then whatever `pipeline_resolve_accounts` asks for over up to four rounds, then `set_clock` from `getEpochInfo` (`crates/pipeline-quoter/src/lib.rs` lines 225 and 334; `docs/INTEGRATOR-GUIDE.md` lines 37 to 39).
  For the measured market that was about ten RPC calls and 0.9 MB.
- Load the router from its deployed ProgramData, not from a local build, so the checks test what is on chain; the probe's sell failure suggests the deployed router is not the `a2d5bfb` source.
- A strategy version is the program id plus the `slot` in its ProgramData header, the slot it was last deployed (`solana-loader-v3-interface 8.1.1`, `src/state.rs` lines 29 to 33; the header is 45 bytes, line 51).
  Pipescope's indexer can watch that account (or poll it) for each registered strategy and queue a Canary run when the slot changes.
- Discovery of strategies and markets is the indexer's job, not the quoter's: on Helius `getProgramAccounts` costs 10 credits and most other calls 1 credit, and the free plan gives 1M credits a month at 10 requests a second (`heliusKnowledge.getHeliusCreditsInfo`, from https://www.helius.dev/docs/billing, fetched 2026-11-09; `alternatives.md` section 4.2).
  500 runs of about ten calls is about 5,000 credits, 0.5% of the free plan; Helius also lists "2 credits/0.1MB" after an allowance, which may apply to the program bytes (unverified).
- The public devnet endpoint is too rate-limited to rely on for discovery (three 429s in one `getProgramAccounts` call); its published limits were not readable on 2026-11-09 (solana.com returned 429 to the fetch).
- In a Container, either the container calls Helius through an outbound handler that adds the key, or the Worker builds the snapshot and posts it in, which lets the container run with `enableInternet = false`.

## Recommendation

- Build the Canary runner as a native Rust binary on `litesvm` and Pipeline's crates (`pipeline-quoter` for quotes, `litesvm` directly for committed buy-then-sell runs), shipped as a linux/amd64 image to a Cloudflare Container on a `basic` instance.
- Drive it from Pipescope's Worker: the indexer queues one job per new strategy version, a Durable Object per strategy version runs it once, and results go to Pipescope's own storage.
- Prefer the Worker building the snapshot and the container running offline, unless the snapshot grows past what a request should carry.
- Keep a small server (Fly.io) as the fallback if Containers misbehave; the binary is the same.
